ip.name: Public IP Address
ip.description: Your IP address is a unique numerical label assigned to your internet connection by your Internet Service Provider (ISP). Think of it like a mailing address for your computer on the global internet.
ip.risk: Websites can use your IP to track your activity across different browsing sessions, determine your general physical location (city/country), and identify your Internet Service Provider.
ip.mitigation: You can hide your real IP address by using a Virtual Private Network (VPN), a secure proxy server, or the Tor browser network.

browser.name: Browser User-Agent
browser.description: Your browser sends a text string called the User-Agent to every website you visit. This string tells the website what browser software you are using, its version, and your device type.
browser.risk: While necessary to display websites correctly, this profile narrows down your identity. When combined with other details, it contributes significantly to a unique browser fingerprint.
browser.mitigation: Privacy-focused browsers (like Brave or Firefox) default to generic User-Agent strings. Alternatively, you can use browser extensions to randomize your User-Agent profile.

os.name: Operating System
os.description: Your operating system (e.g. Windows, macOS, Linux, Android) is the core software managing your computer or phone. This information is broadcast to websites via headers and browser APIs.
os.risk: Knowing your exact OS version helps trackers classify your device and can also expose you to target vulnerabilities specific to that operating system.
os.mitigation: Using privacy configurations that report generic OS versions (e.g. reporting macOS instead of a specific sub-build) helps blend your device in with the crowd.

location.name: Approximate Geolocation
location.description: Websites look up your IP address in global databases that map IP blocks to physical coordinates. This matches your connection node to an approximate city, state, or country.
location.risk: Allows sites to track your region, serve localized ads, block content (geo-blocking), and determine your approximate real-world residency.
location.mitigation: Use a VPN or proxy server to route your connection through a different region, forcing databases to resolve the location of the VPN server instead of your home.

webrtc.name: WebRTC Local IP Leak
webrtc.description: WebRTC (Web Real-Time Communication) is a browser feature that allows voice, video, and peer-to-peer sharing directly inside webpages. To establish connection, it requests your router's local network IP (e.g., 192.168.x.x).
webrtc.risk: A known security vulnerability allows scripts to bypass standard VPN tunnels using WebRTC STUN requests, exposing your real home network IP directly to third-party trackers.
webrtc.mitigation: In Firefox, you can set 'media.peerconnection.enabled' to false in about:config. In Chrome, use extensions like 'WebRTC Leak Shield' or disable WebRTC connection protocols in privacy settings.

dnsleak.name: DNS Tunnel Leak
dnsleak.description: When you type a website name (like google.com), your computer asks a Domain Name System (DNS) server to convert it to an IP address. A DNS leak occurs if these lookup requests bypass your secure VPN tunnel.
dnsleak.risk: Even if your web traffic is encrypted by a VPN, leaking DNS lookups means your ISP (or local eavesdroppers) can see every single domain name you look up and visit.
dnsleak.mitigation: Configure your VPN client to enforce secure DNS leaks protection, or set your system to use public, DNS-over-HTTPS (DoH) encrypted resolvers (like Cloudflare 1.1.1.1 or Google 8.8.8.8).

canvas.name: HTML5 Canvas Fingerprint
canvas.description: The Canvas API is a modern browser feature used to draw graphics. Because different computers process graphic rendering slightly differently due to their graphics card (GPU) and font libraries, drawing a hidden image creates a unique text hash.
canvas.risk: This acts as a cookie-less tracking ID. Even if you clear all cookies and browse in incognito mode, the canvas rendering output remains identical, allowing sites to recognize your hardware profile across domains.
canvas.mitigation: Use privacy extensions like 'Canvas Defender' which inject minor, random pixel noise into the rendering pipeline to break the consistency of the fingerprint hash.

audio.name: Web Audio API Fingerprint
audio.description: The Web Audio API allows browsers to generate and process sound. By synthesizing a high-frequency sound wave in the background, trackers measure minor mathematical variations in how your audio hardware processes mathematical signals.
audio.risk: Like Canvas rendering, this operates as a hardware-specific fingerprint that cannot be erased by clearing standard cookies or using private browser tabs.
audio.mitigation: Disable or restrict Web Audio nodes inside privacy extensions, or use browsers that automatically block or randomize sound synthesis contexts.

vpnOrTor.name: Anonymization Route Audit
vpnOrTor.description: Checks if your IP address matches subnets owned by public cloud hosting systems (like AWS, Azure, DigitalOcean) or known Tor exit relay nodes.
vpnOrTor.risk: Anti-bot firewalls and streaming sites often block hosting IPs and Tor nodes, flagging them as scraper bots, automated spiders, or anonymous proxy bypasses.
vpnOrTor.mitigation: If using Tor is required, configure bridges to obscure exit ranges. If using VPNs, choose providers that route through residential IP networks instead of standard data centers.

proxyHeaders.name: Proxy Forwarding Headers
proxyHeaders.description: When you route web traffic through a proxy server, the proxy often adds forwarding headers (like 'Via' or 'X-Forwarded-For') to inform the destination server about the connection path.
proxyHeaders.risk: Leaking these headers exposes that you are routing your traffic and can leak your real, unproxied IP address, defeating the purpose of the proxy server.
proxyHeaders.mitigation: Use high-anonymity (Elite) proxies that scrub these headers completely before passing requests to destination servers.

userAgentMismatch.name: User-Agent Fingerprint Mismatch
userAgentMismatch.description: Compares your HTTP User-Agent string against the underlying browser APIs (like navigator.platform or screen capabilities). If they don't match, it means a browser is pretending to be a different device.
userAgentMismatch.risk: Commonly flagged by security systems. If a bot or browser extension spoofs the User-Agent header to pretend it is an iPhone, but the screen coordinates or OS variables match a desktop, it is flagged as suspicious spoofing.
userAgentMismatch.mitigation: Ensure your browser spoofers or privacy utilities modify all client-side JavaScript APIs (like navigator.userAgent and navigator.platform) in tandem with HTTP headers to prevent discrepancies.
